title: Send Guard
one_liner: A Slack-style composer that judges every typing pause for secrets, PII, commitments, leaks and tone, then turns the Send button green, amber or red before the next word.
what_it_does: The page renders a pixel-faithful Slack-style workspace for an invented "Northwind" org. The sidebar lists four judged channels: #customer-acme (Slack Connect, external customer), #eng-internal (private, internal), a DM with Jordan Lee (customer) and #public-community (public). The user picks a channel and types in the composer. After a 120 ms typing pause the app sends one request with the channel context, the draft and up to 8 regex-located candidate spans (emails, URLs, key-like tokens, phones, money, dates). The judge returns ten core answers plus one yes/no per span. Code policy (src/lib/policy.ts) turns those answers into send/warn/block with explicit thresholds. Culprit spans get a red wavy underline in the composer via a mirrored highlight layer, a reason line appears under the text, and the Send button turns green, amber ("Send anyway") or red ("Blocked"). A Send Guard pane on the right shows verdict cards, judgment chips with percentages, span verdicts, a regex-only "classic DLP" comparison toggle, a latency HUD (p50/p95, judgments/s, histogram) and a replay table. A Replay button types six prepared scenarios character by character and records expected vs actual verdict.

jev_questions.instructions: Does `draft` contain a secret or credential: an API key, access token, password, private key, connection string, or similar value that grants access to a system?
options: true: The draft includes the actual secret value (even partially redacted values like sk-live-... count).
false: No credential value appears; merely mentioning that keys exist does not count.

jev_questions.instructions: Does `draft` contain personal data about a customer or end user: a named person's email address, phone number, home address, card or account number, government ID, or health details?
options: true: Identifiable personal data about a specific individual appears in the draft.
false: No personal data, or only the author's own company contact details.

jev_questions.instructions: Does the author of `draft` make a binding commitment to the recipient: promising a refund, a specific delivery or fix date, a discount or price, or that a feature will definitely ship?
options: true: A firm promise with words like 'guaranteed', 'will', 'by Friday', 'we'll refund', or a stated price/discount.
false: No promise, or clearly non-committal language ('we're looking into it', 'no ETA yet').

jev_questions.instructions: Given that `channel.audience` describes who can read this message, does `draft` disclose confidential internal company information to people outside the company: unreleased roadmap, internal pricing or margins, unannounced incidents, other customers' names or deals, internal staffing or legal matters?
options: true: Internal-only information is being shared with an external or public audience.
false: Either the audience is internal, or the content is already public / not confidential.

jev_questions.instructions: What is the emotional tone of `draft` toward its reader?
options: Warm: friendly, appreciative, empathetic.
Neutral: professional and matter-of-fact.
Curt: terse, dismissive, or impatient.
Hostile: angry, insulting, sarcastic, blaming, or threatening.

jev_questions.instructions: Considering `channel.name` and `channel.audience`, is `draft` appropriate to send to this audience as written (content, confidentiality, and professionalism together)?
options: true: A reasonable manager would be fine seeing this sent to this channel.
false: Wrong channel for this content, or content a manager would not want this audience to see.

jev_questions.instructions: Does `draft` look unfinished: a sentence that stops mid-thought, a dangling placeholder like TODO or [name], or an obvious missing attachment/link that the text refers to?
options: true: The message is clearly not finished being written.
false: The message reads as complete (even if short).

jev_questions.instructions: Does `draft` contain hedging that undermines the author's own message, such as 'I think maybe', 'not sure but', 'this might be wrong', or apologising for asking?
options: true: Excessive hedging that makes the author sound unsure of a statement they are making.
false: Confident wording, or appropriate uncertainty about a genuinely open question.

jev_questions.instructions: How much legal or compliance risk does sending `draft` to `channel.audience` create for the author's company (contractual promises, regulatory or privacy violations, defamation, admissions of fault, discriminatory remarks)?
options: None: ordinary business communication.
Minor: slightly loose wording a lawyer might tighten.
Material: an enforceable promise, an admission of liability, or personal data shared without need.
Severe: clear regulatory/privacy breach, leaked credentials, defamation, or discriminatory content.

jev_questions.instructions: Taking `channel.audience` into account, should this `draft` be sent as written, sent after the author reviews a warning, or blocked outright?
options: send: Safe, professional, and appropriate for this audience.
warn: Sendable but risky: a commitment, a curt tone, unfinished text, or borderline content the author should double-check.
block: Must not be sent: leaked credentials, customer personal data to the wrong audience, hostile tone to a customer, or confidential information leaving the company.

jev_questions.key: span_N (one per regex span, up to 8)
jev_questions.instructions: The text of `draft` contains the {kind} fragment {text} at `spans` entry "{id}". Given `channel.audience`, is this exact fragment something that should not be sent as-is: a real credential, a customer's personal data, or a specific amount or date the author is committing to?
options: true: This fragment is the (or a) reason the message is risky.
false: This fragment is harmless in context (e.g. the author's own work email, a public URL, a casual mention of a day).

request_cadence: One POST per typing pause (120 ms debounce), with 10 core questions plus up to 8 span questions in a single Jev request. Stale in-flight requests are aborted. Measured run: 81 pauses, 826 judgments, p50 105 ms end to end. Replay types six drafts character by character, so it produces roughly 3 to 8 requests per second.

browser_plan: Port as a route on demo.milliseconds.ai in the milliseconds site style (cloudraker-spring-2026 tokens, fonts and dark theme) while keeping the Slack-style chrome from Shell.tsx, Messages.tsx and Composer.tsx. Replace server/jev.ts with a thin proxy: POST /api/dm1/:route on the site's Cloudflare Worker (site already deploys there). The proxy allowlists yes-no, classify and rate, adds the bearer key from a secret, caps texts to 32 and text to 4000 chars, and passes 429 back with retry-after. The browser builds the bodies. Per typing pause the client sends exactly two requests: call A = POST /yes-no with the shared text and up to 11 core statements plus up to 8 span statements (max 19, under the 32 cap) with shared hints; call B = POST /classify with the send/warn/block labels. On settle (1.5 s idle) it sends two more: /rate tone and /rate legal, which fill the 4-level chips. Throttle: raise the debounce from 120 ms to 400 ms and gate on in-flight, so a new pause never fires while A and B are outstanding; that holds a single typist at about 2 requests/s. Replay: type each scenario at 30 ms per char but judge only at word boundaries and on the final draft, so six scenarios cost roughly 60 requests. A client token bucket (2 tokens/s, burst 4) sits under all of it. On HTTP 429 the client keeps the last verdict, shows a "rate limited, retrying" badge in the pane, backs off with retry-after or 1 s doubling, and pauses replay. Latency HUD keeps clientMs from performance.now() and reads x-inference-ms and x-input-tokens from the proxy response headers for apiMs. Regex-only DLP toggle stays as-is. Add a "How it works" strip that shows the actual call A and call B bodies live, since the demo's job is to sell the API.
risks: No state field in DM1: the channel audience must live inside the text, so the wording of the audience sentence needs a quick eval on the six scenarios (especially the pricing leak in #customer-acme vs the same text in #eng-internal).

Shared when_true/when_false hints across the whole batch lose the per-question criteria Jev had; the inverted is_appropriate_for_audience statement and the tone/legal proxy statements need threshold tuning against the scenario table.

Four calls per settled draft (yes-no, classify, rate, rate) plus replay can hit the org-wide 200 req/min limit when several visitors use the page at once; the client bucket protects one tab only, so the proxy should also count requests per minute and shed load with 429.

Latency story changes: two round trips per pause instead of one; if p50 exceeds the typing pause, the ambient feel degrades to a lagging spellchecker. Measure before shipping and drop call B to settle-only if needed.
The span statements quote the fragment verbatim; a 1000+ char pasted key or URL inflates tokens. Truncate fragment text to 60 chars in the statement.
style.css is 1606 lines of Slack-specific chrome; restyling to milliseconds tokens without breaking the mirrored highlight layer in Composer.tsx is the main UI effort.
